---
title: "Zero-inflated counts"
---

The [Poisson model](poisson-regression.qmd) already assigns positive probability to zero. A zero-inflated model is appropriate only when a second process is proposed to produce additional zeros.

Consider a corpus table that records how often each verb occurs in a particular syntactic frame. A zero may mean that the verb can occur in the frame but did not happen to occur in the finite corpus. It may instead mean that a separate grammatical or lexical process makes the frame unavailable for that verb.

A [**zero-inflated model**](https://appliedstatisticsforlinguists.org/bwinter_stats_proofs.pdf#page=234) represents these as two routes to an observed zero. The model is useful only when the research design or linguistic theory motivates both routes.

## Represent the two routes

Let $q_i$ be the probability that observation $i$ enters a structural zero state. If it does not enter that state, its count follows a Poisson distribution with mean $\lambda_i$. Thus the model contains a structural-zero component and a count component.

The structural-zero component always produces a zero. The count component can produce a zero or a positive count. Thus the probability of an observed zero is

$$
P(Y_i=0)
=q_i+(1-q_i)e^{-\lambda_i}.
$$

The first term is the structural-zero route. The second term is the probability of entering the count component and then receiving a Poisson zero.

For a positive count $y_i$, only the count component is available:

$$
P(Y_i=y_i)
=(1-q_i)
\frac{e^{-\lambda_i}\lambda_i^{y_i}}{y_i!},
\qquad y_i>0.
$$

This structure gives zero inflation its name. The model adds zero probability to the amount already supplied by the count distribution.

## Work through one probability

Suppose $q_i=.60$ and $\lambda_i=2$. The structural-zero component produces a zero with probability $.60$. The count component is entered with probability $.40$, and a Poisson distribution with mean 2 produces a zero with probability $e^{-2}\approx .135$.

The total zero probability is

$$
.60+.40e^{-2}
\approx .654.
$$

The observation has about a 65 percent chance of being zero. About 60 percentage points come from the structural-zero component. The remaining 5 percentage points come from a sampling zero in the count component.

This distinction is latent. When we observe a zero, the data do not label its route. The model infers the relative contribution of the two processes from their predictor relations and from the complete count distribution.

## Give each process its own predictors

The count component can use a log link:

$$
\log\lambda_i
=\mathbf{x}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\beta}.
$$

Corpus size may enter this equation as an exposure offset. Lexical frequency or register may also predict the expected count among observations for which the frame is available.

The structural-zero component can use a logit link:

$$
\operatorname{logit}(q_i)
=\mathbf{z}_i^{\mathsf T}\boldsymbol{\gamma}.
$$

A grammatical classification may enter this equation if it predicts that the frame is unavailable. The predictors need not be identical across the two processes because the processes answer different questions.

For instance, suppose a valency theory separates verbs that license a frame from verbs that do not. That classification may predict the structural-zero component. Among verbs that license the frame, corpus exposure and lemma frequency may predict the count component. Placing every predictor in both components would blur these theoretical roles.

```r
fit <- glmmTMB(
  frame_count ~ log_frequency + offset(log(corpus_size)),
  ziformula = ~ valency_class,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = verb_counts
)
```

The count formula describes the count component. The `ziformula` describes the probability of entering the structural-zero state. The signs have different meanings. A positive coefficient in the count formula raises the expected count among observations generated by the count component. A positive coefficient in the zero formula raises the probability of a structural zero.

## Require a process claim

An unusually large number of zeros does not by itself establish a structural-zero process. A misspecified mean, unrepresented grouping, or a count distribution with greater variance can also make a Poisson model underpredict zeros.

A two-component model requires a substantive account of why some observations enter a state that always returns zero. An excess of observed zeros alone does not supply that account.

In the verb frame case, a grammatical licensing theory may supply that account. In a production experiment, a technical failure that prevents a response from being recorded may supply another. By contrast, an unexplained histogram spike at zero supplies a diagnostic problem but not the required process interpretation.

## Check both components

A fitted zero-inflated model should reproduce the overall zero rate, the zero rate across theoretically relevant predictor values, and the distribution of positive counts. Reproducing only the total number of zeros is insufficient. The model may put the right amount of mass at zero for the wrong groups or distort the count component to compensate.

The interpretation should remain conditional. The structural-zero probability is a model-based estimate of a latent state. It is not an observed grammatical label for each zero. Its plausibility depends on whether the proposed predictors and study design distinguish the two routes.

::: {.callout-note title="Check the process claim"}
A corpus count table has 70 percent zeros. What additional linguistic or design evidence would justify a structural-zero component? Why is the zero percentage alone insufficient?
:::
